#### Materialize or recompute — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** Why materializing is almost always right, and why drift — not lag — is the risk worth designing against.

`foldTo(events, upto)` is one function that answers both "what is it now" and "what was it after event 4". The entire mechanism is a single `continue`, which is why time travel is free when the stream is retained.

`drifts(sourceIsStream, bothWritten)` is worth reading for what it **ignores**: `sourceIsStream` never affects the result. Either direction of derivation is safe; only two independent writers produce drift.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-practice-memory/ch06-practice-memory.svg" alt="Materialize or recompute — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — one fold function, bounded by an index, gives any past table</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-practice-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: one fold function, bounded by an index, gives any past table" width="980">

One `continue` is the whole of time travel: events past index 4 are skipped and `tbl` holds "a" = 16, "b" = 7. No extra storage, no audit table, no second code path — the ability to ask about the past is a consequence of having kept the stream.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — and the same call with no bound gives the present</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-practice-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: and the same call with no bound gives the present" width="980">

Compare the two heap rows: "a" 16 → 24, "b" 7 → 21. "Now" is not a special case of anything — it is `foldTo` with `upto` at the end of the stream, which is why a table-first architecture has to build time travel deliberately and a stream-first one gets it for free.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — eager folds once; lazy folds per query</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-practice-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: eager folds once; lazy folds per query" width="980">

`len(EVENTS) * queries` = 9 × 10 = 90, against eager's 9. Note which factor each depends on: eager is `len(EVENTS)` once, lazy is `len(EVENTS)` per query — so lazy degrades as HISTORY grows, even while the table stays 2 rows.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and drift is a property of having two writers</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-practice-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and drift is a property of having two writers" width="980">

Look at what the function ignores: `sourceIsStream` never affects the answer. Either direction of derivation is safe, and the only thing that produces drift is `bothWritten` — two writers with no function between them. "Which technology" is not the question; "is one view computed from the other" is.

</details>
